paper_title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).

Introduction An LLM agent depends on both its policy model and the harness that manages context, tools, and execution. Improving the harness can raise performance without updating model weights, *This work was done while Xin Yu was an intern at Google. but finding useful changes by hand requires repeated engineering and evaluation (Lin et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026). Recent work automates this process through recursive self-improvement (RSI), using execution feedback to repeatedly propose, evaluate, and select harness edits (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026). Although evolved harnesses can improve perCorresponding author(s): xinyulucas@google.com 2026 Google. As models are updated and agents encounter new tasks, harness optimization often needs to continue beyond that setting. This raises two fundamental challenges. Adapting to new model. Model adaptation arises in two settings: multi-model serving, where one shared harness supports different policy models, and model evolution, where new versions replace earlier ones within model family. Both motivate reusing an evolved harness and its improvement experience instead of independently optimizing harness for every model or release. Yet modifications suited to one policy can interact differently with another, even when the benchmark stays fixed (Yang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026d). In our workspace experiment, an Opus-evolved harness starts at 68.41 on Gemini, below the seed harnesss 73.89 (Figure 4). The optimizer must determine which inherited mechanisms still help and which need revision. Adapting to new data. With the policy fixed, different task distribution can expose failures that source optimization did not address. completion gate that checks whether commands ran successfully, for example, may need to check whether feasible solution is also optimal. In our text-classification experiment, the sourceevolved FewShotAll harness starts at 72.92 on the target suite, below the seeds 75.72 (Figure 3). useful source fix may therefore need revision before it helps the target. In either transition, the evolved harness alone leaves important questions unanswered: why was an edit proposed, what was it expected to fix, and what happened when it was tested? Source optimization produces this evidence, but it need not accompany the harness. Without this history, target optimization may repeat earlier attempts or change inherited components without knowing their purpose. We therefore ask whether the experience gained during source optimization can help the harness adapt to new models or data. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), in which harness optimization continues after benchmark or policy-model change while preserving compatible executable interface. We propose SelfImprovement Memory (SIM) to carry improvement experience alongside the evolved harness (Figure 1). SIM groups selected edits by the harness problems they address and gives the proposer and selector access to their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. It creates entries for new problems and appends further attempts and outcomes to existing ones, helping the optimizer decide which modifications to retain, revise, replace, or remove. Our contributions are as follows: Continual harness optimization. We define cross-dataset continuation with the policy fixed and cross-model continuation with the benchmark and split fixed. Existing harnessoptimization methods can use this setting while retaining their proposal, evaluation, and selection procedures. Self-Improvement Memory. We introduce structured record of harness problems, modifications, and outcomes that conditions both proposal and selection, preserving source experience while incorporating new attempts during target optimization. Controlled evidence across four domains. With matched starting harnesses, round counts, and candidate budgets, Full SIM outperforms harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in six cross-dataset and four Opus-to-Gemini settings. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve 9 of 10 runs, with mean advantage of 2.36 points over harnessonly continuation (p = 0.003). 2. Related Work Recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses. Yu et al. (2026b) survey harness optimization workflows, recursive reuse, and the conditions under which evolved modifications transfer. Meta-Harness and AHE search 2 Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement over harness code using execution traces and scores (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026). Other approaches let the agent modify its own system (Zhang et al., 2026a,b,d) or learn policy for editing harnesses (Shao et al., 2026). SIA instead combines harness edits with updates to the task models weights (Hebbar et al., 2026). Transfer of evolved harnesses. Evolved harnesses can retain their gains on held-out tasks, other models, or downstream benchmarks (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Recent methods encourage transfer through benchmark-disjoint evolution and modular edits (Wu et al., 2026), regularized search (Xia et al., 2026), or separation of general and benchmarkspecific mechanisms (Yu et al., 2026a). Their effectiveness still depends on how the model and harness interact (Yang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026d). PluginRSI also reuses its plugin library in subsequent optimization. Memory of the improvement process. Prior work retains candidate artifacts (Lee et al., im2026), edit histories (Xia et al., 2026), provement graphs (Zhang et al., 2026c), skillrevision records (Li and Hu, 2026), and playbooks (Zhang et al., 2026f). HarnessBank groups candidate harnesses by the problems they address (Luo et al., 2026). Xu (2026) continues multi-task evolution with free-text notes and source replay; Harness2 reuses an improvement library across benchmarks (Xu et al., 2026a). Meta-Skill and Meta2 transfer learned guidance for constructing or editing task-specific harnesses (Qian et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). Continual adaptation also raises retention and interference concerns (Chen et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Within our compute budget, independent RSI repetitions focus on coding; the other domains are evaluated with one run per condition. We study settings with compatible harness interfaces and keep the optimizers planning and search procedures fixed. Our comparisons evaluate SIM as complete procedure, combining inherited memory with updates during target optimization. Future work can extend the evaluation to more repeated runs and longer transition sequences, and explore adaptation of planning, token allocation, and tool interfaces.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: LLM-based optimization agents rewrite harness code in our experiments. The resulting harnesses run inside the benchmarks execution environments, with policy weights fixed and scores computed by frozen verifiers or fixed judging procedure. self-modifying harness could satisfy an evaluator without solving the intended task. We keep held-out feedback away from the optimization agents, identify each benchmarks verifier or judge, and include an accepted edit that failed to repair its target tasks (Appendix F.2). Workspace scores may also reflect biases of the LLM judge. The experiments use existing publicly available benchmarks and datasets.

sections.title: Appendix Contents
sections.content: A E Extended Related Work: harness optimization, transfer, and memory. Benchmarks and Evaluation: datasets, splits, feedback access, and scoring. Experimental Setup: models, seeds, budgets, comparison conditions, and repeated runs. SIM Implementation: how agents read, update, and store SIM. Additional Results: source and target scores, source retention, and ablations. Case Studies: source RSI, continual adaptation, memory records, and transfer patterns. A. Extended Related Work This appendix expands 2 around three questions: how harnesses are improved, how optimization continues after change of setting, and what role memory plays in that process. A.1. How Are Agent Harnesses Improved? Harness RSI optimizes prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and context management around policy model. GEPA uses trajectory reflection and recombination to optimize prompts (Agrawal et al., 2026). Meta-Harness exposes prior implementations, execution traces, and scores through shared filesystem (Lee et al., 2026). AHE makes harness components and modification outcomes observable, checking edit-level predictions against subsequent task outcomes (Lin et al., 2026). In ML development, MLToolBench learns diagnostic tool use through supervised and reinforcement learning (Yu et al., 2026c). Other methods change how improvement Self-Harness combines itself is performed. weakness mining, harness proposals, and regression-based validation (Zhang et al., 2026a). DGM and Hyperagents explore selfmodification and open-ended evolution of agent programs (Zhang et al., 2026b,d); Hyperagents also reports transfer of meta-level improvements across domains. Harness-R1 learns harnessediting policy from failure trajectories using reinforcement learning (Shao et al., 2026), while SIA updates both the harness and the task models weights (Hebbar et al., 2026). Bai et al. (2026) train idea-level critics to screen ML modifications before costly empirical verification. MLToolBench learns task-agent behavior, while the critics learn candidate assessment; SIM preserves edit histories for the proposer and selector. CRSI defines continuation after benchmark or policy change for compatible proposal evaluationselection loops (3.1). A.2. How Does Optimization Continue after Transfer? Transfer of evolved harnesses. AHE evaluates transfer from Terminal-Bench to SWE-bench Verified without re-evolving the harness (Lin et al., 2026); Meta-Harness and PluginRSI report transfer across solver models (Lee et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Several methods aim to improve this transfer. ModularRSI uses benchmarkdisjoint evolution data, contrasts successful and failed trajectories, and directs edits toward recurring deficiencies in functional modules (Wu et al., 2026). RRSI constrains bundled modifications and redirects stalled search toward underexplored components (Xia et al., 2026). Harmony Harness separates general mechanisms from benchmark-specific adaptations (Yu et al., 2026a). The interaction between model and its harness can nevertheless require model-specific adaptation (Yang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026d). Continued optimization. Prior work also reuses improvement experience during further optimization. PluginRSI reuses an evolved plugin library when optimizing from the initial harness (Shi et al., 2026). Xu (2026) continues multi-task harness evolution on new benchmark with free-text evolution notes and source15 Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement task replay. Harness2 retains adopted harnesses and refinement lessons in library and tests its reuse across benchmarks (Xu et al., 2026a). Related settings include task streams and continuous episodes (Karten et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). Adaptive Auto-Harness separates persistent evolution workspace from deployable harnesses, with optional routing among stored branches (Liu et al., 2026). EvoHarnessBench studies retention and adaptation as externally supplied tools, skills, and specialist agents expand (Ke et al., 2026). Evaluating continuation. Held-out evaluation and baselines with matched feedback and inference budgets help distinguish improvements from additional optimization resources (Wang et al., 2026). SEAGym tracks validation, transfer, replay, and cost throughout evolution (Zheng et al., 2026). Studies of shifting task streams and coding benchmarks also document interference and forgetting (Chen et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). We report the evolved harnesss score before and after target RSI, compare memory conditions from the same starting harness with matched round and candidate budgets, and separately track source retention in one coding transition (Appendix E.3). A.3. What Does Memory Store, and Who Uses It? Memory for harness optimization. Keeping improvement history has several precedents. Meta-Harness retains candidate artifacts (Lee et al., 2026); RRSI records hypotheses, diffs, score and cost changes, and acceptance decisions, including rejected edits (Xia et al., 2026). The Causal Improvement Graph links evidence, hypotheses, interventions, and outcomes (Zhang et al., 2026c). SkillHone preserves diagnoses, revisions, and evaluation evidence (Li and Hu, 2026), and Turbo Harness summarizes completed optimization into playbook for instancespecific edits (Zhang et al., 2026f). HarnessBank groups candidates by modified component and diagnosed failure, retaining highperforming harnesses for recombination (Luo et al., 2026). Organizing improvement around problems therefore also has precedent. MetaSkill freezes learned support-design principles to construct harness for each test task (Qian et al., 2026). Meta2 freezes reusable evolution guidance for edits during task execution, resetting the harness between task runs (Yuan et al., 2026). Memory for task solving. Reflexion stores verbal reflections to guide later attempts (Shinn et al., 2023), and Voyager maintains growing library of executable skills (Wang et al., 2024). ExpeL extracts reusable insights from task experience (Zhao et al., 2024); ReasoningBank and ACE retain strategies and lessons (Ouyang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026e). ACE incrementally extends, refines, and deduplicates its playbook from execution trajectories. Memory Transfer Learning compares task-experience representations across coding domains and models, finding abstract insights more transferable than concrete traces in its studied settings (Kim et al., 2026). These memories support the agent executing tasks. SIM in continual harness optimization. SIM supplies the proposer and selector with record organized by harness problem, linking selected modifications to their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context (3.2). The record accompanies the evolved harness across benchmark or model transition and gains new attempts during target RSI. Our comparisons with no SIM and root causes only test this complete procedure, combining inherited history with target-side updates (Appendix E.4.1). B. Benchmarks and Evaluation This section specifies the protocol for the main cross-dataset and Opus-to-Gemini comparisons and the paired coding study. We list the benchmarks and split sizes, explain which feedback can guide optimization, and then define the scoring rules for each domain. The model-generation and shared-harness experi16 Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement ments have additional settings described in Appendices C.5 and C.6, respectively. B.1. Which Benchmarks Do We Use? Benchmarks. We study four domains in which source-evolved harness remains executable in the target environment. For coding, TerminalBench 2.1 (TB2.1) is the source and TerminalBench 4 (TB4) the target (Merrill et al., 2026; Terminal-Bench Team, 2026a,b). For text classification, we use the online classification environment of Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026). The source suite combines LawBench (Fei et al., 2024), the Gretel adaptation of Symptom2Disease (Gretel AI, 2023), and USPTO50k (Schneider et al., 2016). The target suite contains eight datasets absent from source RSI: AG News (Zhang et al., 2015), GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), Banking77 (Casanueva et al., 2020), Financial PhraseBank (Malo et al., 2014), SciCite (Cohan et al., 2019), TweetEval-Hate (Barbieri et al., 2020), Amazon Reviews (Amazon5) (Keung et al., 2020), and SciTail (Khot et al., 2018). For agentic workspace tasks, Harvey LAB (Harvey AI, 2026) is the source. JobBench (Li et al., 2026), GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2026), and APEX-Agents (Vidgen et al., 2026) jointly form the target environment. For engineering design, EngDesign (Guo et al., 2025) is the source and Frontier-Eng (Chi et al., 2026) the target. Table 4 gives the task inventory and rollout allocation. Appendix B.2 defines the split and feedback-access rules; Appendices B.3B.6 detail each domains scoring protocol. In cross-dataset CRSI, Source and target roles. the policy model is fixed while the benchmark changes from the source to the target listed above. In cross-model CRSI, the benchmark and its task split are fixed while the policy changes: source RSI is run with the source policy on that benchmark, and target RSI continues with the target policy. The Opus-to-Gemini comparisons use the corresponding inventory in Table 4 for both stages. B.2. How Are the Splits Used? The tasks (examples for text classification) in Table 4 are split uniformly at random into approximately equal evolve and held-out halves, without stratification by category, difficulty, or source dataset. When benchmark holds an odd number of tasks, the evolve half takes the even count. The two sets are disjoint, and no task or rollout is removed from the scoring denominator after the split. Only evolve-set scores and execution trajectories are available for proposals, selection, SIM updates, and stopping decisions. The tasksolving policy executes the harness on held-out tasks to measure starting, final, and per-round diagnostic scores (4.4). These held-out scores and trajectories are not passed to the harnessoptimization agents. Within these primary comparisons and the paired coding study, the scoring allocation is five rollouts per task on both splits, matched across conditions; the overlapping Frontier-Eng component contributes zero under the rule in Appendix B.6. The reported harness versions, independent-run counts, and statistical comparisons are specified in Appendix C.4. B.3. Coding: Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 4 Environment and metric. Implement adaptive rejection sampling in as /app/ars.R, with input validation and tests. Root cause (c). The agent wrote the whole program in single shell command of about 22.8 KB, exceeding the command-transport limit reported in this run (about 16 KB). The command never ran, so the file was never created and the verifier failed with No ars.R file found. Modification (a). The transport behind the existing run_shell_command tool now splits literal input into chunks of at most 2,048 characters, sends special keys such as Enter as separate key events, and raises an error when send fails instead of failing silently (simplified): MAX_KEY_CHUNK_SIZE = 2048 def _tmux_send_keys(self, keys): cmds = [] for key in keys: if key in SPECIAL_KEYS: # key event cmds.append(f"{prefix} {quote(key)}") continue for chunk in self._split_key(key): cmds.append(f"{prefix} {quote(chunk)}") return cmds Outcome (o). Write compact GPT-2 inference program in (/app/gpt2.c) that loads the weights, decodes greedily, and compiles with gcc -O3 -lm under code-size limit. Root cause (c). Terminus-2 expects JSON response whose keystrokes fields hold shell input. When the model wrote code containing unescaped quotation marks into that field, for example "keystrokes": "...FILE *f = fopen("model.bin", "rb") ;..." json.loads failed and the command was rejected. The parser could already add missing closing braces and strip surrounding text, but not repair quotes inside field. Modification (a). repair step, run only after normal parsing fails, locates the real closing quote of each string field as the one followed by the next expected key (for keystrokes, "duration" or the closing brace) and escapes every quote before it. Source: Execution-Verified Completion Round Edit push, clone Task and evaluation interface. Configure git server so that from my own machine user@server:/git/server, can git and then curl commit hello.html, http://server:8080/hello.html shows hello world. The agent must build four parts that compose: bare repository at /git/server, post-receive hook that deploys to the web root, an SSH-reachable account named user, and an HTTP service on port 8080. The verifier runs outside the container and clones as user over SSH, so setup that works locally is not evidence that the externally visible interface is correct. Observed failure and diagnosis. In the described failing rollout, the agent configured the repository, hook, and web server, read will set up login myself as meaning the account would be provisioned externally, and never created user. The source attempt realizes one of four task-fix predictions; target rounds 5 and 6 realize zero of two and one of two. All attempts retain their outcomes and provenance under the same root-cause hypothesis, including unresolved predictions. mands or errors (Appendix F.2). Core execution handling is retained on TB4. The command-execution routines carry over with the shared container and terminal interfaces, while session checks adapt as described below. The recorded cold-start run does not rediscover the tool-layer changes within eight rounds; after ten rounds it has larger parser without outperforming the inherited harness. Paste-buffer checks adapt to TB4. TB4 exposes failures absent from TB2.1: special key sequences must be normalized for interrupts to take effect, and foreground processes must be identified so that running command is not classified as stalled session. The paste-buffer structure remains, with checks adjusted to these target failures. Completion checks add target criteria. Both inherited harnesses keep completion control while revising the evidence required on TB4. Appendix F.3 follows the selected edits; Appendix F.2 gives the task evidence and the P5/P8 records. Source predicates that no longer fire are pruned rather than re-tuned. Both branches also add reminder triggered by the remaining step budget in their first round, target-specific mechanism that the source did not need. Refusal handling remains inactive. Refusal handling is carried forward but has no triggering tasks on TB4. Its presence alone therefore does not establish transfer benefit or loss. Parser repairs depend on the policy model. The Opusand Gemini-evolved harnesses have near-identical terminal and process structures, which are retained after transfer. Parser repairs instead address model-specific output errors: unescaped control characters, illegal escapes, and truncated responses. Each repair needs checking against the target models outputs. Completion control likewise retains counts of executed commands, discarded blocks, and consecutive rejections, while recalibrating checks Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement for simulated execution and premature completion. The target run also adds format constraints and step-by-step guidance absent from source RSI. F.5.2. Text Classification Source RSI builds structured retrieval. Memory writing moves from no retention (NoMemory) or unstructured storage (FewShotAll) to retrievable indices: multi-granularity BM25 over words, character n-grams, and chemicalformula n-grams, later extended with classbased candidate pools, hard-negative error indices, and class-prototype centrality. Prompt assembly bounds retrieval to the top eight examples with positive BM25 scores, strips benchmark boilerplate from queries before retrieval, and selects contrastive, class-balanced exemplars. Post-processing normalizes data-specific formats, such as SMILES strings for USPTO-50k, because open-vocabulary generation requires exact matches. Retrieval survives with adjusted thresholds. The target suite changes the input types and label spaces. The BM25 index and retriever classes remain intact, while retrieval constants are recalibrated and query sanitization gains delimiters for the new datasets. The routing structure is retained, with rubrics and exemplars rewritten for the target. With SIM, target RSI adds smoothed class quotas and contrastive ordering; class balancing applies to the targets finite label sets rather than the sources open-vocabulary outputs. stays normalization SMILES inactive. SMILES normalization used in source RSI remains inactive on the target suite, whose outputs no longer use that format. The cold-start run independently develops relevance-gated retrieval and bounded context. Indexing transfers while output rules change. Three of four runs evolve BM25 indices from different starting harnesses, using features suited to the input, such as chemical n-grams for SMILES and character bigrams for Chinese legal text. Indexing and query sanitization depend on the input data and carry over across models; retrieval budgets such as top-k are re-tuned. Output rules depend more on policy behavior: the answerfirst schema addresses Geminis truncated reasoning. Target RSI also rewrites inherited rubrics more extensively on Banking77 and GoEmotions than on SciTail and TweetEval-Hate. F.5.3. Agentic Workspace Source RSI adds output handling and audits. Over-long tool outputs are preserved through head-and-tail truncation, with quotas raised threeand five-fold, respectively. one-time audit gate before final_answer can append tool message and return the policy to the loop. deliverable auditor supplies the gate with file names and sizes from candidate output directories. The termination gate survives rubric change. Source RSI and cold-start target run independently add tool message before the same earlyreturn branch, with different predicates and messages. The target gate fires only when no deliverable is registered, files were written during code execution, and the gate has not fired before; the second condition keeps purely conversational tasks from being intercepted. This insertion point depends on the ReAct loop and remains usable when the evaluation rubric changes. Registration checks replace file-system probes. The source probe samples the file system, whereas target failures come from invocation history: files created on disk but never registered through write_file. Target checks therefore use tool-invocation history rather than file-system probes. The target escalates this check in three single-shot tiers: an advisory notice when file saving is detected, mandatory instruction once 75% of the step budget passes without registration, and conditional block at final_answer. Registration checks depend on the evaluator. The registration check assumes that the evalua33 Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement tor credits files registered through write_file; it would need reconsideration for an evaluator that reads output directories directly. Its substring matches over tool arguments (such as /tmp/, .docx, or savefig) also depend on argument formatting. Prompt infrastructure transfers across models. The Opus source run adds editable systemprompt guidelines and six-level severity taxonomy with counterexamples, leaving control flow and tool execution unchanged. The injection mechanism uses message structures, while the taxonomy describes the unchanged evaluator. Geminis cold-start run takes different direction: notice at 80% of the step budget asks it to fill pending fields so that deliverable exists before final_answer; seven later rounds add no improvement in this trace. The timing and wording of such interventions depend on the policys behavior. F.5.4. Engineering Design Source RSI adds design and verification guidance. The source run adds prompt guidance on analytical calculations, self-contained deliverables, tool-failure recovery, and re-reading writIt also imports ten files before completion. syntax parser and tool registry without calling them during source RSI. Target RSI expands checks and context budgets. The tool-registry import is unused in the source harness but becomes the entry point that the Harness Transfer target run uses to enforce centralized output truncation at the registry call. Three target runs independently raise the shared context constants: output-token caps, head and tail lengths, and summarization triggers. The Full SIM target run adapts the sources one-time postgeneration check into checkpoint protocol that writes intermediate artifacts exceeding the baseline score to disk, protecting them from unannounced timeouts. The cold-start target runs retained edits are limited to prompt changes: reconstructing the objective from the evaluation script, embedding self-tuning optimization code in deliverables, and clamping outputs with fallback to the baseline implementation. SIM retains the source guidelines in this trace. The Harness Transfer target run inherits the source guidelines but reverts them to the seed prompt in its first round, whereas the Full SIM target run retains and extends them throughout. This pair retains similar code structures but differs in whether the inherited guidance is preserved. Deliverable checks survive model changes. deliverable tracker that records deliverable state independently of model output transfers without refactoring, and check that blocks final_answer when deliverable was modified but not re-executed transfers unchanged. Budget prompts emerge as wall-clock triggers in an Opus run (every 600 s, at most three times) and step-budget ratios in Gemini runs (0.8 and 0.75). Both use the gate before final_answer, with checks on different state variables. The recorded zero-score rates differ between Opus (0.09%) and Gemini (4.49%); intervention thresholds therefore need checking for each policy. Handlers for missing sandbox binary remain idle where the environment is fully provisioned. Interfaces explain much of the observed reuse. Across these cases, benchmark changes alter the evidence needed for completion, while model changes alter how the harness handles policy failures. With the benchmark fixed, model change leaves the success criterion intact but can require different detection and guidance. Stable interfaces favor reuse; output repairs and intervention thresholds need checking against the target setting. F.6. What Do the Cases Tell Us about SIM? The cases suggest four roles for SIM in continuing harness optimization. Earlier rationale informs what to retain. In engineering, the SIM run retains and extends Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement inherited guidance, while harness-only continuation reverts it (F.5.4). Recording why an edit was made gives the optimizer basis for assessing its continued relevance, beyond its presence in the inherited harness. transferable rationale can require different implementation. The coding runs inherit the same completion gate, but the SIM run extends it to check target-specific requirements (F.3). The need for completion evidence carries over; what counts as sufficient evidence changes. This illustrates how earlier reasoning can guide adaptation without treating the source implementation as fixed. New outcomes add evidence to an existing diagnosis. P3 links source diagnosis to further target interventions and their outcomes (F.4). Keeping these attempts together lets later rounds inspect which remedies were tried, under which settings, and which predictions remain unresolved. The reusable experience includes the evidence behind diagnosis, not only its name. Experience remains available after an edit is replaced. P8 retains the selected blocking attempt and its unresolved predictions after later edits change the behavior (F.2). The final harness alone would omit this part of the search history. SIM keeps the attempt, its diagnosis, and its unresolved outcome together as the harness changes.
